Oak leaf cluster
An oak leaf cluster is a ribbon device to denote preceding decorations and awards consisting of a miniature bronze or silver twig of four oak leaves with three acorns on the stem.
The bronze oak leaf cluster represents one additional award, while the silver oak leaf cluster is worn in lieu of five bronze oak leaf clusters.
In Germany, the German oak is the national tree of Germany, thus oak leaves are a prominent symbol on most German military orders.
During World War II, the Knight's Cross of the German Iron Cross could be awarded with the additional distinction of oak leaves (mit Eichenlaub).
Of the 7,313 awards of the Knight's Cross, only 882 received oak leaves.
After World War II, Iron Crosses awarded previously could be worn by the recipient provided the swastika was replaced by oak leaves.
The Bundeswehr awards the Cross of Honour for Bravery for extraordinary bravery.
The Cross of Honour for Bravery differs from the Badge of Honour by an adornment in the shape of stylized double oak leaves.
Furthermore, it was featured on the Pfennig in Germany and since the introduction of the euro in 2001 it is used on the obverse side of the German euro coinage.
In earlier times, the Pour le Mérite, the highest military order in the Kingdom of Prussia, could also be awarded with oak leaves.
A civil version of the order, for accomplishments in the arts and sciences, still exists in the Federal Republic of Germany.
In Commonwealth countries, a bronze oak leaf signifies a Mention in Despatches, and is worn as a gallantry award in its own right, rather than to signify multiple instances of campaign service.
Oak leaves are a common motif on military symbols in Turkey because of the famed longevity of the oak tree.

Santa Fe (Belgrano) railway station
Santa Fe is a former railway station in the city of Santa Fe de la Vera Cruz in Santa Fe Province, Argentina.
Having been closed in March 1993 after the Government of Argentina closed all the long-distance services in Argentina, the station was reopened by the local Municipality as a convention center.
The Santa Fe station was part of the large CN's network that connected the province with cities such as Buenos Aires, Córdoba, Santiago del Estero Province, Tucumán, and Chaco among others.
FA operated trains to Jujuy and Salta provinces, being Santa Fe one of the intermediate stops on the route.
On March 10, 1993, president Menem signed the decree for which all the long distance passenger services were definitely closed, with Santa Fe being included among them.

The entire Belgrano Railway lost all its services carried until then, with the exception of freight transport that continued operating through Belgrano Cargas, a consortium that took over Belgrano Railway in 1999.
In 2008, the Cencosud consortium featured a project to build a shopping mall in the former station, with a cost of A$ 100 million and the creation of 1,200 job positions.
In 2013, a recently created company, Belgrano Cargas y Logística took over the lines previously operated by Belgrano Cargas.
After analyzing the proposal, the National Government granted Cencosud a concession to exploit the Belgrano station for commercial purposes.
With the station still owned by the National government and concession already given to Cencosud, the municipality started works of refurbishment in January 2009 at an initial cost of A$326,000.
On the other hand, the Municipality of Santa Fe featured its own project that consisted in remodelling the station with no commercial purposes (unlike the proposal by Cencosud).
In April that same year, the Administración de Infraestructura Ferroviarias (ADIF) summoned the Municipal government to cease works.

Finally in July 2010 both, the ADIF and the municipality reached an agreement by which the municipal government received the station in concession for a term of 10 years (with the possibility to be extended).
The remodelled Belgrano station building was put into service again as multi-purpose building that included both, convention and administrative centres, and the seat of local Secretary of Tourism.

In 2014, the state-owned Operadora Ferroviaria Sociedad del Estado took over passenger services in Argentina, reestablishing some services to Santa Fe Province but only to Rosario Sur and Rufino stations.
As of June 2015, there are no plans to run trains to Santa Fe station.

The Boxers, fueled by anti-foreign and anti-Christian sentiments, targeted foreigners and Chinese Christians, causing approximately 900 soldiers, sailors, marines, and civilians from various nations, along with about 2,800 Chinese Christians, to seek refuge in the Legation Quarter.
The Qing government, initially ambivalent, ultimately supported the Boxers following international military actions.
The failure of the siege and the subsequent occupation of Peking by foreign powers effectively ended the Boxer movement and increased foreign influence and intervention in China.
The siege lasted 55 days, marked by intense combat and a brief truce, until an international relief force arrived from the coast, defeated the Qing forces, and lifted the siege.
In 1900, there were eleven legations in the quarter as well as a number of foreign businesses and banks.
The twelve or so Christian missionary organizations in Peking were not in the Legation Quarter, but rather dispersed around the city.

Lincoln Ellsworth
Lincoln Ellsworth (May 12, 1880 – May 26, 1951) was an American polar explorer, engineer, surveyor, and writer.
His parents were Eva Frances (née Butler) and James Ellsworth, a wealthy coal mine owner and financier.
Ellsworth and his sister moved to Hudson, Ohio, to live with his grandmother.
His academic performance was poor, and he subsequently enrolled at Columbia University School of Mines and studied civil engineering.
After dropping out of college in 1903, Ellsworth climbed the Andes with a fraternity brother.
In 1905, he worked as an assistant engineer of a gold mine in Teller Alska.
In 1906, he returned to his father's coal mine, working as an engineer.
During World War I, he served in the United States Army and trained as an aviator.
Elsworth led the trans-Andean topographic survey from the Amazon River basin to the Pacific Ocean in Peru for Johns Hopkins University in 1924.
Ellsworth's father funded US$100,000 ($1.84 million in 2025) to Roald Amundsen's 1925 attempt to fly from Svalbard to the North Pole.
Ellsworth senior died in Italy on June 2, 1925, while waiting for news of his lost son.
In early March 1926, under the headline "Across the Pole by Dirigible", The New York Times announced the Amundsen-Ellsworth Expedition.
Ellsworth made four expeditions to Antarctica between 1933 and 1939 using as his aircraft transporter and base, a former Norwegian herring boat that he named Wyatt Earp after his hero.
The aircraft, named Polar Star, was a Northrop Gamma outfitted with skis.
On November 23, 1935, Ellsworth discovered the Ellsworth Mountains of Antarctica when he made a trans-Antarctic flight from Dundee Island to the Ross Ice Shelf.
During the flight, his aircraft ran out of fuel, forcing a landing near the Little America camp set up by Richard Byrd.
The two men were discovered on January 16, 1936, after almost two months alone at Little America.
Because of a faulty radio, he and his pilot, Herbert Hollick-Kenyon, were unable to notify authorities about the landing.
The two men were declared missing, and the British research ship Discovery steamed out from Melbourne, Australia to search for them.
In 1927, the Boy Scouts of America made Lincoln Ellsworth an Honorary Scout, a new category of Scout created that same year.
In 1928, Ellsworth was awarded a Congressional Gold Medal that honored both his 1925 and 1926 polar flights.
The American Museum of Natural History created the Lincoln Ellsworth exhibit about his Arctic and Antarctic voyages in 1933; it remains open to the public as of 2024.
The United States Postal Service issued a commemorative stamp in his honor in 1988.
In 1919, the high school athletic teams of Hudson High School in Hudson, Ohio, were nicknamed "The Explorers" after Ellsworth.
Ellsworth died of heart failure at his home in New York City on May 26, 1951, at the age of 71.

Pfäffikon Castle is a castle in the municipality of Freienbach of the Canton of Schwyz in Switzerland.
Between 1233 and 1266 Abbot Anshelm von Schwanden replaced the old granary with stone tower which was designed as a watch tower, granary and residence.
In 1299 the Prince-Abbot Johann von Schwanden added walls, ramparts and a moat to the tower during the Marchenstreit conflict between the Schwyz and the Abbey over grazing rights.
On the night of Epiphany in 1314 a mob from Schwyz attacked the Abbey attempting to destroy the land and tax records.
By 1359 the castle was being used as the Abbot's summer residence as well as for its original purposes.
In the 15th century Abbot Burkard von Weissenburg-Krenkingen (1418-1438) expanded the castle and changed its name to Weissenburg.
In 1480 the election of a new Abbot for the Abbey took place at Pfäffikon.
In 1528 the castle was renovated and the walls and moat were repaired.
Abbot Joachim Eichhorn (1544-1569) built a new Gothic chapel and expanded the granary in the castle.
In 1577 a fire destroyed much of the Abbey and the village of Einsiedeln.
The monks and villagers moved to the Castle for 7 months until the Abbey and their homes were repaired.
Around 1760 Eichhorn's granary expansion was demolished and replaced with another residential wing.
Following the 1798 French invasion and the creation of the Helvetic Republic Pfäffikon Castle was heavily damaged and declared the property of the Canton of Linth.
Following the collapse of the Republic and the 1803 Act of Mediation the castle was returned to the Abbey and once again became religious property.
In 1820 the remainder of the curtain wall was demolished while the tower, chapel and residential wings were rebuilt.
In 1839 the rotten tower roof and overhand were replaced with the current roof.
In 1928 the chapel was renovated and in 1986-88 the chapel, tower and moat were repaired and renovated.
The portal is Gothic, while the interior was decorated in the Baroque style in 1780-85, which was partly replaced in 1893-95.
The walls are made of massive stone blocks and are 2.3 m (7.5 ft) thick at the base, tapering to 1.4 m (4.6 ft) thick on the top floor.

Liberalism in Poland
Liberalism has been a notable ideology in Poland for hundreds of years.
Poland has officially been a liberal democracy since 1989, though its status has been challenged as a result of illiberal reforms in the 2010s and 2020s.
The first major advocate of liberal ideas in Poland was Stanisław Konarski, who criticized the liberum veto in his work On an Effective Counsel in the 1760s.
Over the following decades, the Monitor covered the details of social and cultural life in Poland while spreading ideals of a national identity independent of the aristocracy.
Józef Wybicki wrote for the Monitor at this time, and his writings reflected his studies of Montesquieu.
Hieronim Stroynowski wrote the handbook The Study of Natural and Political Law, Economics and the Law of Nations, which emphasized individual freedoms, private property, contract, and free trade.
The rule of Stanisław August Poniatowski brought the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth to an end in the 18th century during the Polish Enlightenment.
Stanisław Staszic was a prominent philosopher during the Polish Enlightenment, advocating elections and physiocracy.
The Constitution of 3 May 1791 implemented many of these legal ideas and set up a constitutionalist system in the final years of the Commonwealth.

Hugo Kołłątaj recognized the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth as a single unitary state with national sovereignty and argued that the contributions of artisans and tradesmen contributed to a country's wealth as well as agriculturists.
The Duchy was dissolved following the fall of the French Empire in 1815, and the Kingdom of Poland was set up as an autonomous territory of the Russian Empire.
Its leader, Stanisław Węgrzecki, advocated early liberalism under a "monarch without despotism".
Liberal ideas were spread by professors Jan Śniadecki and Krystyn Lach-Szyrma as well as the Freemasons.
The Kaliszanie presented a limited opposition to the conservative majority in government during this time.
The ideology of the Kaliszanie was inspired by the political ideas of Benjamin Constant and the economic ideas of Adam Smith.
As with many central European countries, Polish liberals were accepting of liberalism in a monarchy instead of republicanism throughout the 19th century.
Following the November Uprising in 1831, Poland lost much of its autonomy and Polish liberalism was further impaired.
Intellectual and cultural developments also contributed to the advancement of liberal ideas in Poland during this time, typically through periodicals and the spread of Hegelianism.
The Revolutions of 1848 represented a major advancement for liberalism in Europe, but the Polish uprising did not succeed in freeing Poland from subjugation.
The previously suppressed Russian partition of Poland experienced a revival of liberalism in the late 1850s.
Polish liberals in the 1860s were represented by the Whites and opposed by the socialist Reds.
Whites such as Józef Ignacy Kraszewski and Karol Ruprecht supported Polish independence but believed that a premature insurrection would harm the Polish people.
Liberalism in the 1860s and 1870s was primarily spread through liberal periodicals, such as Gazeta Narodowa and Dziennik Literacki.
A new group of radical positivists and rationalists led by Aleksander Świętochowski continued to influence Polish liberalism.
In the 1880s, Polish liberals began to allow for an increased role of government in their philosophy.
Going into the 20th century, liberalism had grown stronger in the Austrian partition while it had been replaced by conservatism in the Prussian partition.
Politics became increasingly radical in the Russian partition, and a faction of liberals led by Świętochowski responded with the "progressive democracy" movement, opposing mob rule and partisanship.
Other ideas taken on by Polish liberalism in the 1900s included feminism and anti-clericalism.
The most prominent liberals at this time were Kraków School economists, advocating individualism over nationalism and collectivism.
As a result of the primarily agricultural nature of the Polish economy and the relative lack of industrialization, state intervention became commonplace to spur growth.
Liberal government ended in the Second Polish Republic following the coup in 1926.
The invasion of Poland in 1939 ended liberal government in the country and brought about 50 years of one-party rule.
During World War II, Poland was occupied by Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union.
When the war ended, the Polish People's Republic was set up as a Communist client state of the Soviet Union.
Liberalism in Communist Poland was preserved by a contingent of Polish citizens along with the Catholic Church.
Poland ascended to NATO in 1999, and NATO initiated a series of reforms to place the Polish military under civilian control.

Law and Justice (PiS), which has been a major party in Poland since 2005, has been described as "illiberal", and Poland's government under Law and Justice has been described as an "illiberal democracy".
Following the establishment of a PiS-controlled government in 2015, a form of illiberal legalism was set up in Poland.
Liberalism is also been associated with secularism in Poland, and it is opposed by highly religious voters and highly Catholic voters in particular.
During the 19th century, Polish liberalism was divided among many factions based on different philosophies, including positivism, rationalism, and radicalism.
Modern Polish liberalism has been described as being combined with elements of conservatism and republicanism following the end of Communist rule.
Liberals in Poland also support the right to abortion, freedom of religion, and LGBT rights.

Liberalism was first developed in Poland as a response to the Polish–Lithuanian monarchy, and it continued to develop in response to the partition of Poland through the 19th century and Communist rule in the 20th century.

Liberalism further set up itself as the predominant political ideology of Poland in the second half of the 19th century, and it was strengthened through the spread of positivist philosophy and the economic ideas of Józef Supiński.

Satyabhama (IAST: Satyabhāmā) , also called Satrajiti, is a Hindu goddess and the third queen consort of the Hindu god Krishna.
Satyabhama is described as an incarnation of Bhumi, an aspect of Lakshmi.

Satrajita, who secured the jewel from the sun-god Surya and would not part with it even when Krishna, the king of Dvaraka, asked for it saying it would be safe with him.

Jambavan, known for his role in the Ramayana, killed the lion and gave the jewel to his daughter Jambavati.
Krishna, in order to remove the stain on his reputation, set out with his men in search of the jewel and found it in Jambavan's cave, with his daughter.
Jambavan attacked Krishna thinking him to be an intruder who had come to take away the jewel.

At his request, Krishna sieged the city of Narkasura with the assistance of his mount, Garuda, along with his wife Satyabhama.
Having rescued the 16,000 women, Krishna married them upon their request to restore them of their honour in society, making them his junior wives.
In the tale, Satyabhama is regarded to have prided herself on the love Krishna had for her, and her grasp over his heart.
Narada, with his way with words, tricked her into accepting a vrata ritual, where she had to give Krishna away in charity to Narada, and reclaim him by offering the weight of Krishna in wealth.
After donating Krishna to Narada, Satyabhama arranged for a big scale (tula) to be put up, and sent for her huge treasure of gold and jewellery.
Narada warned her that if she was unable to balance the scales, he would be forced to auction Krishna as a slave to someone else.
The entire weight of the jewellery of Krishna's wives did not succeed in balancing the scales.
In the end, Rukmini was able to resolve the situation by offering a single tulasi leaf upon the other scale, after chanting a prayer, which balanced the scales.

While there are different versions in different texts as to why the weighing was arranged, the story of the tulasi leaf placed by Rukmini being worth more in weight than that of Satyabhama's wealth is a common ending.
Going beyond the Himavat, they took up their abode in a place called Kalpa.
Narada visits Krishna's inner palace and sees Satyabhama seated on Krishna's throne, looking into a mirror and adorning herself.
When she reacts contemptuously to Narada's ascetic appearance reflected near her face, Narada resolves to humble her pride.
Rather than abducting her or falsely accusing her, he chooses co-wife rivalry as his means, leading to the introduction of Rukmini in the Jain Pradyumna narrative.

The Latvian-speaking majority remained largely alienated from the church up to the beginning of the 18th century when the pietistic movement of Moravian (Herrnhut) Brethren reached Latvia.

After religious freedom returned to Latvia in 1988, the Church underwent a leadership change: figures accused of collaborating with the Soviet authorities were removed from church administration, and a new archbishop was elected.
Along with the Church of Sweden, the ELCL now claims full apostolic succession.

Bent (sometimes stylised as BENT) is a 1979 stage play written by Martin Sherman.
When the play was first performed, there was only a trickle of historical research or even awareness about the Nazi persecution of homosexuals.
One evening, much to the resentment of his boyfriend Rudolph Hennings (Rudy), he brings home a handsome Sturmabteilung man, Wolfgang Granz (Wolf).
Unfortunately, it is the night that Hitler orders the assassination of the upper echelon of the Sturmabteilung corps, to consolidate his power.
Wolf is discovered the next morning and killed by SS men in Max and Rudy's apartment, and the two have to flee their home.
Greta is a drag queen; she ran her own gay club, which is newly shut down (implicitly due to, at the time, new Paragraph 175 enforcements).
Greta explains that the SS approached her for information about Wolf, and that she took them to Max and Rudy's apartment.
As a result, Max and Rudy are found in a forest tent-colony and arrested by the Gestapo.

Max's uncle Freddie, who is also gay, but lives a more discreet life with rent boys to satisfy his desires, has organized new papers for Max to flee to France where homosexuality is legal, but Max refuses to leave Rudy behind.
Another prisoner on the train, wearing a pink triangle patch, explains the patch system during the Holocaust to Max and tells Max that he must show no sentiment towards Rudy.
The officer makes Rudy crush his glasses, and then orders Rudy to be taken, presumably to be killed for his poor eyesight.
Rudy is beaten within an inch of his life, all the while Max tries to ignore his screams.

Constitutionalist Revolution

The Constitutionalist Revolution of 1932 (also called the Paulista War or Brazilian Civil War) was the uprising by the population of the Brazilian state of São Paulo against the Revolution of 1930, when Getúlio Vargas assumed the nation's presidency.
Vargas was supported by the people, the military and the political elite of Minas Gerais, Rio Grande do Sul and Paraíba.
The movement grew out of local resentment over Vargas' rule by decree, unbound by a constitution, in a provisional government.
The revolution's main goal was to press Vargas' provisional government to adopt and abide by a new constitution, since Prestes was prevented from taking office.
As the movement developed and resentment of Vargas and his revolutionary government grew deeper, it came to advocate the overthrow of the federal government.
The uprising began on July 9, 1932, after four protesting students were killed by government troops on May 23.
During the following months, the state of São Paulo rebelled against the federal government.
Counting on the support of the political elite of two other powerful states, Minas Gerais and Rio Grande do Sul, São Paulo's politicians expected a quick war.
The expected support did not materialize, and São Paulo's revolt was overwhelmed by force on October 2, 1932.
In 87 days of fighting (July 9 to October 4) there were 934 official deaths, although unofficial estimates report up to 2,200 dead; many cities in the state of São Paulo experienced damage.

In spite of its military defeat, some of the movement's main demands were granted by Vargas: the appointment of a non-military state governor, the election of a Constituent Assembly, and the enactment of a new constitution in 1934.

The new constitution was short-lived; in 1937, amidst growing extremism on the left and right, Vargas dissolved the National Congress and enacted another constitution which set up the Estado Novo after a coup d'état.
July 9 marked the beginning of the revolution, and is a holiday and the most important civic date of the state of São Paulo.
Paulistas (as residents of São Paulo are known) consider the Revolution of 1932 the greatest movement of their civic history, and it was the first major revolt against the Vargas government.

Minaean language
The Minaean language (also Minaic, Madhabaic or Madhābic) was an Old South Arabian or Ṣayhadic language spoken in Yemen in the times of the Old South Arabian civilisation.
The main area of its use may be in the Al Jawf region of North-East Yemen, primarily in the Wādī Madhāb.
Most of texts in this language were composed by the Minaeans, but the other civil-temple communities of the Wādī Madhāb (Nashshan, Kaminahu, Ḥaram, and Inabba') also used it as a literary medium.

One peculiarity of Minaean is that it writes the phoneme /s/ in foreign names as /ṯ/ (e.g., Delos becomes dlṯ), but still keeps the phoneme distinct in native words.
Minaean, like the other non-Sabaean languages also has a temporal conjunction mty ("when").

The Sengoku period (戦国時代, Sengoku jidai; Japanese pronunciation: [seŋ.ɡo.kɯ (d)ʑiꜜ.dai, -ŋo.kɯ-] lit.
'Warring States period') was an era of civil war, political fragmentation and social change in Japanese history.

Its end is variously dated to Oda Nobunaga's entry into Kyoto in 1568, the fall of the Ashikaga shogunate in 1573, Toyotomi Hideyoshi's unification of Japan in 1590, the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600 or the Siege of Osaka in 1615.
The period overlaps with the later Muromachi period and, under broader definitions, the Azuchi–Momoyama period.
The Ōnin War devastated much of Kyoto and accelerated the decline of the Ashikaga shogunate.
Although the Ashikaga shōguns remained in office until 1573, their ability to control the provinces became increasingly limited.
Portuguese merchants introduced the arquebus in 1543, after which Japanese weapons manufacturers began producing firearms domestically.
The arrival of Francis Xavier in 1549 was followed by the spread of Christianity, particularly in parts of Kyushu.
Nobunaga entered Kyoto in 1568 and ended the Ashikaga shogunate five years later.
After his death in 1582, Hideyoshi continued the process of consolidation and brought the remaining major regional powers under his authority by 1590.
Following Hideyoshi's death, Tokugawa Ieyasu defeated his principal rivals at Sekigahara, became shōgun in 1603 and destroyed the Toyotomi house in 1615.
During the Nanboku-chō period, the emergency hanzei system permitted military authorities to divert part of the income from specified estates to support armies.
His son Ashikaga Yoshimochi maintained much of this authority, but a succession crisis followed the death of Yoshimochi's son, Ashikaga Yoshikazu, in 1425.
When Yoshimochi died without a surviving heir in 1428, senior officials selected the next shōgun by lot from among four of Yoshimitsu's sons who had entered religious life.
In 1441, Akamatsu Mitsusuke assassinated Yoshinori during a banquet in what became called the Kakitsu incident.
The traditional starting date is the outbreak of the Ōnin War in 1467, because the conflict severely weakened the political order centered on the Ashikaga shogunate in Kyoto.

Other interpretations begin with the Kyōtoku incident in 1454, which initiated decades of warfare in the Kantō region, or the Meiō incident in 1493, after which powerful military families repeatedly deposed, installed, and competed for control of Ashikaga shōguns.
The Kyōtoku incident began when Ashikaga Shigeuji, the Kantō kubō and principal Ashikaga authority in eastern Japan, ordered the killing of his deputy, Kantō kanrei Uesugi Noritada, in 1454.
The murder divided the warrior families of the Kantō between Shigeuji and the Uesugi-led coalition supported by the Kyoto shogunate.
Although a settlement was reached in 1482, the conflict left the Kantō politically divided and is therefore sometimes treated as the regional beginning of the Sengoku period.
Shigeuji withdrew to Koga, from which he and his successors became called the Koga kubō, while the shogunate set up a competing Ashikaga authority at Horigoe.
The Ōnin War grew from several interconnected disputes rather than from the Ashikaga succession alone.
Rival branches of the Hatakeyama and Shiba families contested their respective leaderships, while Hosokawa Katsumoto and Yamana Sōzen competed for influence within the shogunate.
The uncertain succession of Shōgun Ashikaga Yoshimasa, involving his brother Ashikaga Yoshimi and infant son Ashikaga Yoshihisa, became entangled with these existing rivalries.
By 1467, the competing groups had assembled large armies in Kyoto under coalitions conventionally called the Eastern and Western armies.
The alliances were not fixed: participants changed sides, pursued local disputes, and continued fighting after Katsumoto and Sōzen both died in 1473.
The conflict in Kyoto ended in 1477 when Ōuchi Masahiro and the remaining Western forces departed, but the disputes that had fueled it were not resolved.
The Ōnin War did not immediately eliminate either the Ashikaga shogunate or every set up provincial government.

Local communities and religious organizations also formed leagues called ikki, including the provincial league that governed southern Yamashiro Province after 1485 and the Ikkō-ikki that took control of Kaga Province in 1488.
Some recent scholarship, particularly in Japan, places the beginning of the Sengoku period at the 1493 Meiō incident.
The Kyōtoku incident of 1454 is sometimes used because it began prolonged warfare and divided Ashikaga authority in the Kantō region.

The conventional date is 1467, when the Ōnin War began in Kyoto, while another interpretation favors the Meiō incident of 1493, when Hosokawa Masamoto deposed Shōgun Ashikaga Yoshitane and installed Ashikaga Yoshizumi.
An early ending date is 1568, when Oda Nobunaga entered Kyoto and installed Ashikaga Yoshiaki as shōgun.
Nobunaga's move to Azuchi Castle in 1576 is another proposed transition point because it gave the later Azuchi–Momoyama period part of its name.
The year 1573, when Nobunaga expelled Yoshiaki from Kyoto, is used when the end of the Sengoku period is equated with the termination of the Ashikaga shogunate and the Muromachi period.
Another group of dates associates the period's end with the political unification of Japan.
In 1587, Toyotomi Hideyoshi issued the sōbujirei, which prohibited daimyō from conducting private wars.

His defeat of the Later Hōjō clan in the Odawara campaign of 1590 brought the last major independent regional power under his authority and is frequently treated as the completion of national unification.

Hideyoshi's death in 1598 reopened the struggle for national supremacy, however, making 1590 an unsuitable endpoint for definitions that include the subsequent conflict between the Toyotomi and Tokugawa coalitions.
The Toyotomi family nevertheless retained substantial autonomy at Osaka Castle until its destruction in the Siege of Osaka in 1615.
Consequently, 1600 represents Tokugawa military supremacy, 1603 the institutional foundation of the new shogunate and 1615 the elimination of its last major rival.
Tokugawa Ieyasu defeated his principal rivals at the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600 and was appointed shōgun in 1603, establishing the Tokugawa shogunate.
The Sengoku and Azuchi–Momoyama periods therefore overlap under many systems of periodization.

The latter generally describes the governments and unification campaigns of Nobunaga and Hideyoshi, beginning in 1568, 1573 or 1576 and ending with Hideyoshi's death, Sekigahara or the establishment of the Tokugawa shogunate.
Yoshitane supported Hatakeyama Masanaga in the continuing succession conflict within the Hatakeyama clan, but their policies brought them into opposition with kanrei Hosokawa Masamoto.
While Yoshitane and Masanaga were campaigning against Hatakeyama Yoshitoyo in Kawachi Province in 1493, Masamoto seized control of Kyoto in the Meiō incident.
As kanrei, Masamoto had been one of the shogunate's most senior officials, but his power after 1493 extended beyond the customary authority of that office.
Yoshitane was deposed and replaced by Ashikaga Yoshizumi, while Masanaga was defeated and killed.
Yoshitane escaped captivity and continued to claim the shogunate, creating two rival Ashikaga lines supported by competing military coalitions.
The kanrei is sometimes compared with the shikken of the earlier Kamakura shogunate, but the two offices developed in different political systems and were not direct equivalents.

Masamoto had no biological children and adopted three prospective heirs from different families: Hosokawa Sumiyuki, originally a son of the aristocratic Kujō family; Hosokawa Sumimoto, from the Awa branch of the Hosokawa; and Hosokawa Takakuni, from another collateral branch.
In 1507, retainers supporting the disinherited Sumiyuki assassinated Masamoto in an event called the Eishō no sakuran (永正の錯乱, Eishō disturbance).
Sumiyuki did not personally kill Masamoto and did not retain power for long; supporters of Sumimoto and Takakuni defeated and killed him several weeks later.
In 1508, Takakuni joined former shōgun Yoshitane and Ōuchi Yoshioki, whose army advanced on Kyoto from western Japan.
Fighting continued between the rival Yoshitane–Takakuni and Yoshizumi–Sumimoto coalitions, including the Battle of Funaokayama in 1511.
After Yoshioki returned to his western provinces in 1518 and Sumimoto died in 1520, Takakuni exercised increased control over the shogunate.
When Yoshitane broke with him in 1521, Takakuni installed Yoshizumi's son Ashikaga Yoshiharu as the twelfth shōgun.
Sumimoto's son Hosokawa Harumoto, supported by Miyoshi Motonaga, renewed the struggle against Takakuni.
Their forces expelled Takakuni and Yoshiharu from Kyoto in 1527, although control of the capital continued to change hands.
Takakuni subsequently allied with Uragami Muramune, but their coalition was defeated by Harumoto and Motonaga at the Battle of Daimotsu in 1531.
Takakuni and Muramune were both killed, leaving Harumoto as the principal Hosokawa power in the central provinces.
Harumoto soon came to regard Motonaga's growing military influence as a threat.
In 1532, he encouraged armed adherents of the Ikkō-shū to attack Motonaga, who was defeated and forced to kill himself at Sakai.
Although Harumoto temporarily dominated the shogunate, his dependence upon powerful retainers anticipated the subsequent rise of Motonaga's son, Miyoshi Nagayoshi.
The Mōri initially operated between the much larger Ōuchi clan, based in Suō and Nagato, and the Amago clan, based in Izumo.
Motonari gained an early military reputation at the Battle of Arita-Nakaide in 1517 and became head of the Mōri clan in 1523 following the death of his young nephew.
Motonari initially cooperated with the Amago but transferred his allegiance to the Ōuchi in 1525.

His survival depended partly upon Ōuchi support: when Amago Haruhisa invaded Aki and besieged Motonari at Yoshida-Kōriyama Castle in 1540, an Ōuchi relief army helped force the Amago withdrawal in January 1541.
His eldest son, Mōri Takamoto, became heir to the main Mōri house, while his second and third sons were adopted into two important Aki families as Kikkawa Motoharu and Kobayakawa Takakage.
The cooperation of the Mōri, Kikkawa and Kobayakawa houses gave the clan access to additional territory, soldiers and naval forces.
Motonari strengthened his position through marriage, adoption and alliances as well as warfare.
The well-known “lesson of the three arrows”, in which Motonari supposedly demonstrated to his sons that three arrows bound together could not easily be broken, is a later legend.

The political balance in western Japan changed in 1551 when Sue Harukata, a senior Ōuchi retainer, overthrew Ōuchi Yoshitaka in the Tainei-ji incident and installed Ōuchi Yoshinaga as the clan's nominal head.
Motonari initially maintained relations with the new regime but broke with Sue in 1554.
In the Battle of Itsukushima in 1555, Mōri forces defeated Sue's larger army and Sue killed himself.
Mōri forces then advanced into the eastern Ōuchi territories, and Yoshinaga was forced to kill himself in 1557.
The collapse did not transfer the entire Ōuchi realm to Motonari: the Mōri took its eastern territories, while the Ōtomo clan extended its influence over parts of the west and northern Kyushu.
Mōri forces gradually isolated the Amago stronghold of Gassantoda Castle, which surrendered in 1566 after an extended campaign.
Motonari formally transferred the clan leadership to Takamoto but continued to direct major political and military decisions.
After Takamoto's death in 1563, Motonari supported his grandson Mōri Terumoto as heir while Motoharu and Takakage assumed leading military and administrative roles.
Motonari died at Yoshida-Kōriyama Castle in 1571 at the age of 74.
In 1546, Hōjō Ujiyasu defeated a coalition led by Uesugi Norimasa and Uesugi Tomosada in the Battle of Kawagoe.
Tomosada was killed and Norimasa was eventually driven from Kōzuke Province, allowing the Later Hōjō clan to become the leading power in much of the Kantō region.
Uesugi Kenshin was born Nagao Kagetora and belonged to the Nagao family, hereditary deputies of the Uesugi governors of Echigo Province.
Describing this process as the complete “unification” of Echigo in 1551 is misleading, because Kenshin continued to face resistance and negotiate with powerful local retainers throughout his rule.
Uesugi Norimasa sought refuge with Kagetora after his defeat by the Later Hōjō and encouraged him to intervene in the Kantō.
In 1559, Kagetora travelled to Kyoto, where he received an audience with Shōgun Ashikaga Yoshiteru and visited the imperial court.
In 1561, Norimasa adopted Kagetora into the Uesugi clan and transferred to him the Uesugi family name and claim to the office of Kantō kanrei.
Kagetora subsequently used several names, including Uesugi Masatora and Terutora, before becoming best known by his Buddhist name, Kenshin.
Kenshin and Ujiyasu concluded an alliance in 1569 in response to their common conflict with Takeda Shingen, although the agreement did not permanently settle their territorial rivalry.
Their armies confronted one another during five campaigns around Kawanakajima in 1553, 1555, 1557, 1561 and 1564.
After a prolonged campaign, Nanao Castle fell to the Uesugi in 1577, bringing most of Noto Province under Kenshin's authority.
His forces expanded through Etchū Province and intervened in a succession conflict within the Noto Hatakeyama clan.
Later accounts describe the subsequent Battle of Tedorigawa as a major Uesugi victory, but the size of the armies, course of the fighting and extent of the Oda defeat are uncertain.
Kenshin died suddenly at Kasugayama Castle in 1578 at the age of 48 under Western age reckoning, or 49 under the traditional Japanese system.
Earlier forms of gunpowder weaponry were already known in Japan, and some historians have suggested that matchlocks from other parts of Asia may have arrived before 1543.
Nevertheless, the weapons acquired at Tanegashima provided the model for the Japanese firearm commonly called the tanegashima.
Japanese craftsmen quickly reproduced the weapon, and manufacturing centers had developed at Negoro, Sakai and Kunitomo by the middle of the 1540s.
The adoption of firearms formed part of a broader expansion and reorganization of Sengoku armies, but it did not by itself create the ashigaru or cause the consolidation of Japan.
Oda Nobunaga became particularly associated with the organized battlefield use of firearms, most famously at the Battle of Nagashino in 1575.
The allied Oda and Tokugawa army used matchlock troops and field fortifications against the attacking Takeda forces.
Later accounts credited Nobunaga with deploying 3,000 gunners in rotating ranks, but the scale and tactical novelty of this arrangement are disputed.
Nagashino was therefore an important large-scale use of matchlocks in the field, rather than the first use of firearms in Japan or a single revolutionary event that transformed Japanese warfare.
His control of Owari and Mino provided the territorial and economic base from which he could intervene in the politically important Kinai region.
In 1568, Nobunaga marched to Kyoto in support of Ashikaga Yoshiaki, brother of the murdered shogun Ashikaga Yoshiteru.
After overcoming the Rokkaku clan and driving the Miyoshi forces from the capital, Nobunaga secured Yoshiaki's installation as the fifteenth and final shogun of the Ashikaga shogunate.
Nobunaga defeated him at Makishima Castle and expelled him from Kyoto in 1573, effectively ending the Ashikaga shogunate, although Yoshiaki continued to claim the title of shogun until 1588.
Nobunaga and Tokugawa Ieyasu defeated the Azai–Asakura army at the Battle of Anegawa later that year, but the two clans continued resisting until 1573.
His 1570 invasion of Echizen Province was abandoned after his brother-in-law Azai Nagamasa allied with Asakura Yoshikage and threatened the Oda army's route of retreat.
Resistance from Buddhist institutions and leagues of armed believers presented a longer challenge.
Nobunaga conducted three campaigns against the Ikkō-ikki strongholds at Nagashima, finally destroying them in 1574.
The war against Ishiyama Hongan-ji, led by Kennyo, lasted from 1570 until a negotiated evacuation of the fortress in 1580.
In 1575, Nobunaga and Ieyasu defeated Takeda Katsuyori at the Battle of Nagashino.
Nobunaga also constructed Azuchi Castle, which became the administrative and symbolic center of his expanding regime.
By 1582, Nobunaga directly governed central Japan and exercised authority over a wider coalition of subordinate lords, but he had not yet unified the entire country.

Nobunaga later ordered campaigns conducted by his principal commanders: Shibata Katsuie expanded Oda authority in the Hokuriku region, Hashiba Hideyoshi advanced against the Mōri in western Honshu and Akechi Mitsuhide campaigned in Tamba Province.
The Mōri remained powerful in western Honshu, the Uesugi controlled territory in the north and the Chōsokabe, Shimazu and Later Hōjō remained independent.
During the final campaign against the Takeda clan, Oda forces conquered Kai and Shinano and Katsuyori committed suicide.
Later that year, while staying at Honnō-ji in Kyoto with only a small entourage, Nobunaga was attacked by Akechi Mitsuhide.
Hideyoshi subsequently defeated Mitsuhide and continued the process of unification begun under Nobunaga.
Under Nobunaga, Hideyoshi participated in campaigns in central Japan and was subsequently placed in command of the Oda advance against the Mōri clan in western Honshu.
When Nobunaga was killed by Akechi Mitsuhide in the Honnō-ji Incident in June 1582, Hideyoshi was besieging Bitchū Takamatsu Castle.
At the subsequent Kiyosu Conference, Hideyoshi supported Nobunaga's infant grandson Sambōshi as the formal Oda heir while distributing the former ruler's territories among the leading Oda retainers.
Hideyoshi defeated their coalition at the Battle of Shizugatake in 1583, after which Katsuie and Nobutaka committed suicide.
In 1584, Hideyoshi fought Tokugawa Ieyasu and Oda Nobukatsu in the Komaki–Nagakute campaign.
The conflict ended after Hideyoshi negotiated a separate peace with Nobukatsu; Ieyasu formally submitted to Hideyoshi only in 1586.
His forces compelled Chōsokabe Motochika to surrender most of Shikoku in 1585 and defeated the Shimazu clan during the Kyūshū campaign of 1587.
In 1590, an enormous coalition of subordinate lords besieged the Later Hōjō clan at Odawara, while other Toyotomi forces captured its remaining fortresses.
The suppression of the Kunohe rebellion in 1591 consolidated Toyotomi authority in northern Honshu.
Although regional daimyō retained control of their domains, they were incorporated into a national political order centered on Hideyoshi.
Because his ancestry prevented him from becoming shogun, Hideyoshi obtained authority through the imperial court.
His 1588 sword hunt ordered the confiscation of weapons from farmers and religious institutions.
Hideyoshi's government conducted nationwide cadastral surveys, standardized the measurement of agricultural production and redistributed domains according to assessed rice yields.
Together with restrictions on occupational mobility, these measures accelerated the separation of warriors from cultivators and strengthened the daimyō governments through which Hideyoshi ruled.
In 1592, Hideyoshi invaded Korea with the stated objective of advancing into Ming China.

Following the birth of his son Toyotomi Hideyori in 1593, Hideyoshi ordered Hidetsugu to commit suicide in 1595 and executed many members of Hidetsugu's household, eliminating the only adult Toyotomi successor.
Before his death at Fushimi Castle on September 18, 1598, Hideyoshi set up the Council of Five Elders and other governing bodies to protect the five-year-old Hideyori.
Japanese forces withdrew from Korea after Hideyoshi's death, but the political settlement he created soon fractured, culminating in Tokugawa Ieyasu's victory at the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600.
After the Komaki and Nagakute campaign of 1584, Ieyasu eventually acknowledged Hideyoshi's supremacy and participated in the campaign against the Later Hōjō clan in 1590.

By the time of Hideyoshi's death in 1598, Ieyasu possessed the largest domain in Japan and was the most powerful member of the Council of Five Elders, which had been appointed to govern until the young Toyotomi Hideyori reached adulthood.
Although the transfer removed him from the politically important Kinai, it gave Ieyasu control of a large and economically productive territory.
Tensions developed between Ieyasu and other members of the Toyotomi government as he arranged political marriages and alliances without the required collective approval.
In 1600, the dispute divided many of Japan's daimyō into two coalitions.
The conflict culminated in the Battle of Sekigahara on October 21, 1600.
His opponents accused him of attempting to appropriate Toyotomi authority, while Ieyasu presented his actions as necessary to preserve political order.
The Eastern Army supported Ieyasu, while the Western Army was organized principally by Ishida Mitsunari and nominally headed by Mōri Terumoto.
The defection or nonparticipation of several Western commanders, most notably Kobayakawa Hideaki, contributed to Ieyasu's victory.
Sekigahara did not immediately abolish the Toyotomi regime, but it left Ieyasu as the dominant military authority in Japan.
In 1603, Emperor Go-Yōzei appointed Ieyasu shōgun, formally establishing the Tokugawa shogunate at Edo.

Ieyasu transferred the title to his son Tokugawa Hidetada in 1605, demonstrating that the office would be inherited by the Tokugawa family, but he continued to exercise effective authority from Sunpu Castle.
The Toyotomi family nevertheless retained Osaka Castle and considerable wealth and prestige under Hideyori.
Relations between the two houses deteriorated as former Toyotomi retainers and other opponents of Tokugawa rule assembled at Osaka.
During the winter and summer campaigns of the siege of Osaka in 1614–1615, Tokugawa forces captured the castle and destroyed the remaining Toyotomi leadership.
Hideyori and his mother Yodo-dono died as the castle fell, and Hideyori's young son was subsequently executed.
The Miyoshi, originally important retainers of the Hosokawa, became the dominant power in the Kinai under Miyoshi Nagayoshi.
In Owari, branches of the Oda clan, which had served as deputies of the Shiba clan, gradually appropriated provincial authority.
Hōjō Sōun, more accurately known during his lifetime as Ise Sōzui or Ise Shinkurō, was traditionally portrayed as a poor wandering warrior who rose entirely through his own ability.
Later scholarship has set up that he belonged to the Ise family, which served the Ashikaga shogunate, and possessed important connections to the Imagawa clan.
His son Hōjō Ujitsuna subsequently adopted the Hōjō name, and the dynasty now called the Later Hōjō remained a major Kantō power until its defeat by Toyotomi Hideyoshi in 1590.
Through service under Oda Nobunaga, he advanced from a low-ranking retainer to a commander entrusted with major campaigns.
The Yamashiro ikki expelled two competing Hatakeyama armies from southern Yamashiro in 1485 and administered the area through an association of local warriors and communities until 1493.
In Kaga Province, followers of the Hongan-ji, allied local warriors and disaffected former retainers overthrew shugo Togashi Masachika in 1488.
Hongan-ji adherents became increasingly dominant during the sixteenth century and maintained substantial control until Oda forces conquered the province between 1575 and 1582.

The Smoking Gun
The Smoking Gun is a website that posts legal documents, arrest records, and police mugshots on a daily basis.
Most of The Smoking Gun's content is obtained through Freedom of Information Act requests to federal, state, and local law enforcement agencies, and from public records such as court documents.
The cable network truTV, formerly Court TV, purchased The Smoking Gun, as well as the website Crime Library, in 2000.
A series of the same name premiered on Court TV in 2005, which featured some of the site's stories and assorted sketch humor, using string puppets.
The site published its second book, The Dog Dialed 911: A Book of Lists from The Smoking Gun, in October 2006.
From March 2008 until January 2011, on truTV, The Smoking Gun sponsored a cable television series called The Smoking Gun Presents: World's Dumbest...
The series was originally called World's Dumbest Criminals, but was re-titled World's Dumbest..
William was a cast member on the show alongside Smoking Gun writer Andrew Goldberg.
As of January 2011, the program was re-titled again to truTV Presents: World's Dumbest...
In June 2014, The Smoking Gun was sold back to William Bastone.

In August 2009, the site outed members of Pranknet, a virtual community notorious for tricking hotel and fast-food restaurant employees into setting off fire alarms, engaging fire-suppression systems, and engaging in humiliating acts.
In 2006, the site uncovered widespread fabrication in James Frey's alleged memoir A Million Little Pieces.

In 2010, the site revealed financial irregularities in Yéle Haiti, a charitable foundation set up by rapper Wyclef Jean, soon after he publicized its successful fundraising for disaster relief following the 2010 earthquake in Haiti.
As reported by The New York Times, the foundation had failed to file several years of tax returns.
Later, it was found to have illegally diverted funds to the personal use of Jean and some of his family.

Virgin birth of Jesus
The Islamic understanding of this event comes from the Quran, which also asserts the virgin birth of Jesus.

In Christianity and Islam, it is asserted that Jesus of Nazareth was conceived by his mother Mary solely through divine intervention and without sexual intercourse, thus resulting in his virgin birth.
In accordance with these beliefs, Jesus had just one biological parent; Mary's husband Joseph was his father only in the familial and legal sense.
Though not biologically related, Jesus being Joseph's adoptive son is cited as linking him to the Davidic line.
The Christian understanding is that the birth of Jesus by a virgin woman was made possible by the Holy Spirit of the Trinity.
Christians regard the doctrine as an explanation of the combination of the human and divine natures emanating from Jesus Christ.
According to Richard Bell, the Quran derives its narrative from the 2nd-century Protoevangelium of James.

When his mother Mary had been engaged to Joseph, but before they lived together, she was found to be with child from the Holy Spirit. 19: Her husband Joseph, being a righteous man and unwilling to expose her to public disgrace, planned to dismiss her quietly.

20: But just when he had resolved to do this, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream and said, "Joseph, son of David, do not be afraid to take Mary as your wife, for the child conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit.
The virgin's name was Mary. 30: The angel said to her, "Do not be afraid, Mary, for you have found favor with God.

32: He will be great, and will be called the Son of the Most High, and the Lord God will give to him the throne of his ancestor David. 33: He will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end." 34: Mary said to the angel, "How can this be, since I am a virgin?" 35: The angel said to her, "The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the child to be born will be holy; he will be called Son of God.
36: And now, your relative Elizabeth in her old age has also conceived a son; and this is the sixth month for her who was said to be barren.
The two agree that Mary's husband was named Joseph, that he was of the Davidic line, and that he played no role in Jesus's divine conception, but beyond this they are very different.

Matthew does not mention any census, shepherds, or presentation in the temple, and implies that Joseph and Mary were living in Bethlehem at the time of the birth, while Luke does not mention any magi, flight into Egypt, or massacre of the infants, and states that Joseph lived in Nazareth.

Luke introduces Mary as a virgin, describes her puzzlement at being told she will bear a child despite her lack of sexual experience, and informs the reader that this pregnancy is to be effected through God'...
Other scholars argued Semitisms occur throughout the Gospel of Luke, not just in chapters 1–2, with especially dense concentrations in chapters 4, 5, 7, 9–10, 13–19, and 24.
The most likely cultural context for both Matthew and Luke is Jewish Christian or mixed Gentile/Jewish-Christian circles rooted in Jewish tradition.
Nevertheless, there are many contemporary churches in which it is considered orthodox to accept the virgin birth, but not heretical to deny it.

In the New Testament, narratives that include the virgin birth appear only in Matthew 1:18–25 and Luke 1:26–38, and the modern scholarly consensus is that it rests on slender historical foundations, though conservative scholars maintain its historicity.
Such stories are less frequent in Judaism, but there too was a widespread belief in angels and divine intervention in births.

Luke's virgin birth story is a standard plot from the Jewish scriptures, as for example in the annunciation scenes for Isaac and for Samson, in which an angel appears and causes apprehension, gives reassurance, and announces the coming birth, the mother raises an objection, and the angel gives a sign.
Both Matthew and Luke are compositions dating from the period AD 80–90, though this still places them within the lifetimes of eyewitnesses, including Jesus's own family.
The earliest Christian writings, the Pauline epistles, do not contain any mention of a virgin birth and simply state that he was "born of a woman" and "born under the law" like any Jew.
In the later epistle 1 Timothy, the author urges that "certain persons" should not "occupy themselves with myths and endless genealogies which promote speculations..." 1 Timothy 1:4.
Though the author of the Gospel of John is confident that Jesus is more than human, he makes no reference to a virgin birth to prove his point.

Joseph dominates Matthew's and Mary dominates Luke's narrative; James Barker suggests that Luke intended to supplement Matthew’s nativity by adding Mary’s perspective to Matthew’s Joseph, while Brown views it as no more than a pious deduction.
Davies argue that Matthew presents with minimal redaction a unified and preexisting infancy narrative.

Matthew presents the ministry of Jesus as largely the fulfilment of prophecies from the Book of Isaiah, and Matthew 1:22-23, "All this took place to fulfill what had been spoken by the Lord through the prophet: 'Look, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son...'", is a reference to Isaiah 7:14, "...the Lord himself shall give you a sign: the maiden is with child and sh...
According to Mark Goodacre, the Gospel of Matthew did not base the virgin birth on a mistranslation of Isaiah.
As such, this story is without precedent either in Jewish or pagan literature.
The Ebionites, a Jewish Christian sect, saw Jesus as fully human, rejected the virgin birth, and preferred to translate almah as "young woman".
The 2nd century gnostic theologian Marcion likewise rejected the virgin birth, but regarded Jesus as descended fully formed from heaven and having only the appearance of humanity.
By about AD 180 some Jews suggested that Jesus had been illegitimately conceived by a Roman soldier named Pantera or Pandera, whose name is likely a pun on parthenos, virgin.
The story was still current in the Middle Ages in satirical parody of the Christian gospels called the Toledot Yeshu.
The Toledot Yeshu contains little historical material, and was probably created as a tool for warding off conversions to Christianity.
The Annunciation became an element of Marian devotions in medieval times, and by the 13th century direct references to it were widespread in French lyrics.
The Eastern Orthodox Church uses the title "Ever Virgin Mary" as a key element of its Marian veneration, and as part of the Akathists hymns to Mary which are an integral part of its liturgy.
The Annunciation is one of the most frequently depicted scenes in Western art.

The doctrine is often represented in Christian art in terms of the Annunciation to Mary by the Archangel Gabriel that she would conceive a child to be born the Son of God, and in Nativity scenes that include the figure of Salome.
Annunciation scenes also amount to the most frequent appearances of Gabriel in medieval art.
The depiction of Joseph turning away in some Nativity scenes is a discreet reference to the fatherhood of the Holy Spirit and the virgin birth.

Jainism in Tamil Nadu
Jainism has an extensive history in the Indian state of Tamil Nadu, although practiced by a minority of Tamils in contemporary times.
According to the 2011 India Census, Jains represent 0.12% of the total population of Tamil Nadu, and are of the Digambara sect.
Tamil Jains are primarily concentrated in northern Tamil Nadu, in the districts of Viluppuram, Kanchipuram, Vellore, Tiruvannamalai, Cuddalore and Thanjavur.
Inscriptions dating back to 8th century CE were found in Tiruchirappalli narrating the presence of Jain monks in the region.
The Trilokyanatha Temple in Kanchipuram and Chitharal Jain Temple were built during the reign of the Pallava dynasty.
The Sittanavasal Cave and Samanar Malai are Jain complexes that were built during the reign of Pandyan dynasty.

On 9 December 2016, Park Geun Hye, the president of South Korea, was impeached as the culmination of a political scandal involving interventions to the presidency from her aide, Choi Soon-sil. 234 members of the 300-member National Assembly voted to impeach and temporarily suspend Park's presidential powers and duties.

The court upheld the impeachment in a unanimous 8–0 decision on 10 March 2017, removing Park from office.

The regularly scheduled presidential election was advanced to 9 May 2017, and Moon Jae-in, former leader of the Democratic Party, who Park had narrowly defeated in the 2012 presidential election, was elected as Park's permanent successor.
Park was formally sentenced to 24 years in prison on 6 April 2018 after being found guilty of abuse of power and coercion.
According to Article 65 Clause 1, if the president, prime minister, or other state council members violate the Constitution or other laws of official duty, the National Assembly can impeach them.
Clause 2 states the impeachment bill must be proposed by one third, and approved by a majority of members of the National Assembly for passage.
After impeachment, the final decision on whether to remove the impeached from office rests with the Constitutional Court of Korea.
By the Constitutional Court Act of 1988, the Constitutional Court must make a final decision within 180 days after it receives any case for adjudication, including impeachment cases.
The last president to be subject to impeachment was Roh Moo-hyun, who was impeached by the National Assembly in 2004 and was suspended from duties for two months.
In that case, the Constitutional Court acquitted Roh and restored him to power, with the South Korean public by and large in support of Roh.
On 25 October 2016, Park apologized to the nation in a televised address from the Blue House for giving Choi access to draft speeches during the first months of her presidency.

Media investigations also reported that Choi and President Park's senior staff members, including both Ahn Jong-bum and Jeong Ho-sung, have allegedly used their influence to extort ₩77.4 billion ($60 million) from Korean chaebols—family-owned large business conglomerates—and set up two culture- and sports-related foundations, Mir and K-sports foundations.
On 31 October, Choi Soon-sil was arrested by prosecutors, having concluded that there was enough evidence for an indictment.

Park made a second apology on 4 November, pledging to take responsibility if she was found guilty, and a third apology on 29 November, calling for the National Assembly to decide the manner of her departure, but this was rejected by the opposition-controlled legislature.
Protests across South Korea began on 26 October with Park's approval rating dropping to 4%, and according to an opinion poll, as of 9 December 78% of South Koreans supported her impeachment.
President Park appointed Park Young-soo, former head of the Seoul High Prosecutors' Office, as a special prosecutor to investigate the allegations on 30 November.
Choi's daughter Chung Yoo-ra was also sought by prosecutors as a key witness.
When she did not return to Korea for the investigation, an Interpol warrant was put out for her arrest.
In late 2016 and early 2017, the German Federal Police began investigating Choi and Chung for money laundering.
The response to the Sewol ferry sinking accident that occurred on 16 April 2014 also contributed to Park's declining presidential ratings.

Park's Saenuri Party initially preferred Park to voluntarily step down in late April, but with mounting protests, the ruling party became divided on whether Park should step down voluntarily or be impeached.

The 300-member National Assembly was scheduled to vote on an impeachment bill on 9 December, at the end of the legislative session.
The opposition parties pledged to resign their seats in the National Assembly if the impeachment motion failed to pass.
On 9 December, the National Assembly approved the impeachment motion by a vote of 234 in favour and 56 against in a secret ballot.
As a result of the motion's passage, President Park's powers and duties were suspended for up to 180 days while the Constitutional Court of Korea considered the validity of the impeachment motion.

President Park held a final cabinet meeting acknowledging the impeachment motion and apologised for causing uncertainty, before Prime Minister Hwang Kyo-ahn assumed presidential powers and duties at 19:30 Korean Standard Time, on an interim basis.
Some 40 family members of the victims of the sinking of MV Sewol looked on as lawmakers cast their secret ballots.

Under the Constitution, if the impeachment were upheld, new elections would have had to be held so a new president could take office by October 2017 at the latest.

SMS Blitz (1882)
SMS Blitz was an aviso of the German Kaiserliche Marine (Imperial Navy) built in the early 1880s.
The Blitz class featured a number of innovations in German warship design: they were the first steel hulled warships and the first cruiser-type ships to discard traditional sailing rigs.

In the 1880s, these duties included conducting demonstrations of torpedo boat capabilities under the direction of Alfred von Tirpitz, then the head of torpedo development in the German Navy, who frequently used Blitz as his flagship.

The ship's activities during World War I are unclear, with one historian stating she was employed as a coastal defense vessel until 1915 and then as a tender until the end of the war in 1918, and another trio of historians who state that she remained in service as a tender for the fleet's battleships through 1917, took part in Operation Albion in the Baltic Sea in October 1917, and was slated to participate in Operation Schlußstein, the occupation of St.
Blitz was struck from the naval register in March 1921 and subsequently broken up.

In 1892–1893, the ship was rearmed with six 8.8 cm (3.5 in) SK L/30 pattern quick-firing guns in single mounts and three 35 cm torpedo tubes, one in the bow and one on each broadside, all submerged in the hull.
Initial testing lasted until 30 April and design defects that were discovered during the trials necessitated corrections at the shipyard.
The ship was recommissioned on 22 April 1884 and assigned to the armored division to serve as the unit's aviso.
A second round of trials were held between 24 July and 15 December, after which she was decommissioned.

The ships conducted training maneuvers in the North and Baltic Seas that year, and from 20 to 24 December, they visited Frederikshavn, Denmark during a cruise through the Kattegat and Skagerrak for a test of torpedo boat endurance.
From 6 to 22 August, Blitz led the division on a cruise to Trondheim, Norway as another demonstration of torpedo boats' ability to operate at sea.

During the summer maneuvers in August and September, she led her torpedo boats with an armored warship division composed of Bayern, Friedrich Carl, and Hansa, and an unarmored division that comprised three old sail corvettes and Pfeil.
Starting in March 1886, Tirpitz led the flotilla on training exercises that lasted until July.
Thereafter, Blitz and her accompanying torpedo boats joined the annual fleet maneuvers as III Division.
Following the conclusion of the maneuvers in September, Blitz and the flotilla visited Christiana, Norway.
On the way back, Blitz accidentally rammed the British steamer Oakland on 10 September; she was able to rescue only two crewmen from Oakland before she sank.
After repairs were completed, she joined the fleet for maneuvers that lasted until 23 September.
There, she embarked Princes Wilhelm and Heinrich and took them to Britain for the Golden Jubilee of their grandmother Queen Victoria on 20 June.
Blitz and the torpedo boats left Britain on 26 June and arrived in Kiel two days later.
Training exercises were then held in the Baltic and North Seas, during which Blitz and the torpedo boats formed IV Division, and on 28 September she was decommissioned.
In July, she accompanied the fleet that the newly crowned Kaiser Wilhelm II on a state visit to Tsar Alexander III of Russia from 14 to 31 July.

Blitz was decommissioned in late September; the outbreak of the Abushiri revolt in German East Africa prompted the navy to consider sending Blitz to join the East Africa Squadron, but the proposal was abandoned.

The year 1890 passed without incident; Blitz escorted Wilhelm II on a visit to Norway and she was present for the ceremonial transfer of the island of Helgoland from British to German control (by way of the Heligoland–Zanzibar Treaty).
During the 1891 training year, the torpedo-boat flotilla was joined by the Training Squadron for exercises.
Blitz was used to train boiler room personnel in 1892, and over the winter of 1892–1893, the ship was modernized with new quick-firing guns.
Blitz initially served as a training ship for boiler room crews in 1894, and beginning on 18 April she became the flotilla leader for I Flotilla.
During the 1894 maneuvers, which postulated a two-front war against France and Russia, Blitz remained in the Baltic to defend against the simulated Russian attack.
During a night attack practice in late July, Pfeil and the torpedo boat D4 accidentally collided and Blitz had to tow the torpedo boat back to port.
The next year followed the same pattern and passed without incident until August, when she was relieved as the flotilla leader by D2.
Blitz thereafter served as the tender for the artillery training ship Mars for the rest of 1895.
In 1896, the ship served as a flotilla leader and later as a dispatch boat for the corvette Blücher, which served as the fleet flagship during training exercises that year.
The ship served as a tender for the pre-dreadnought battleship Kurfürst Friedrich Wilhelm, the flagship of I Squadron in 1897.
During the summer maneuvers that year, Blitz and Pfeil served in the simulated hostile squadron.
The ship was assigned to the Naval Artillery Inspectorate and was used to train auto-cannon crews from February to April 1899.
Beginning on 16 September, she was employed as a fishery protection vessel, along with the old aviso Zieten.
During this period, she patrolled off the mouth of the Humber, the Dogger Bank, and in the southern North Sea.
During training maneuvers on 10 May, the torpedo boat S71 struck Blitz and seriously damaged her rudder, forcing her to go to the Kaiserliche Werft (Imperial Shipyard) in Kiel for repairs.
Beginning on 25 September, she became a tender for the fleet's battleships, a role she filled for the next fifteen years.
In 1904, Blitz was transferred support the battleships of I Battle Squadron, though during the summer training exercises she reverted to Kaiser Wilhelm II.
The year 1905 followed the same routine, with the ship alternating between I Squadron and Kaiser Wilhelm II, though she also served temporarily with the scouting unit.
The years 1907, 1908, and 1909 passed uneventfully and Blitz remained in Germany during the fleet cruises to the Atlantic and to Spain in those years.
In need of another overhaul by 1910, Blitz went into dry dock at the Kaiserliche Werft in Danzig for repairs that lasted from 30 April to 1 August.
The ship accompanied the fleet on its cruise to Norway from 6 to 25 June, which included stops in Odda and Balestrand.
The other ships included in the special unit created to carry the operation out included the battleships Nassau, Ostfriesland, and Thüringen.
The ships entered the Baltic on 10 August but the operation was postponed and then cancelled, with the special unit being dissolved on 21 August.
Both agree that she was struck from the naval register on 8 March 1921 and then broken up in Wilhelmshaven.
Blitz was 78.43 meters (257 ft 4 in) long overall and had a beam of 9.90 m (32 ft 6 in) and a maximum draft of 4.07 m (13 ft 4 in) forward.

The ship's propulsion system was rated for 2,700 metric horsepower (2,700 ihp) and provided a top speed of 15.7 knots (29.1 km/h; 18.1 mph) and a range of approximately 2,440 nautical miles (4,520 km; 2,810 mi) at 9 knots (17 km/h; 10 mph).

Additionally, Altneuland also highlights Herzl's commitment to social equality and the idea of a multicultural Jewish society.
The novel portrays a Jewish state where Jews and Arabs live together in harmony, reflecting Herzl's belief in the importance of coexistence and mutual respect between different communities.
The novel directly reflected Herzl's political philosophy represented through a new form, literature.

Altneuland, at the time of the rise of Zionism as a political movement in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, saw the emergence of a new form of Jewish nationalism that sought to establish a Jewish state in Palestine began to prevail.

1886 Charleston earthquake
The earthquake and its aftershocks caused damage to buildings in cities such as Savannah and Augusta, Georgia, as well as Columbia, South Carolina, more than 100 miles from Charleston.
Scientists have classified it as an intraplate earthquake, and said that it had an estimated moment magnitude of 6.9–7.3 and a maximum Mercalli intensity of X (Extreme).
The earthquake was so severe that outside the immediate area, there was speculation that the Florida peninsula had broken away from North America.
Similar faults are found all along the east coast of North America.
Roger Bilham and Susan Hough studied historical mapping projects published between 1884 and 1919 and discovered a 1 m (3 ft 3 in) uplift at Summerville along the South Carolina Railroad.
Photographic evidence of the South Carolina Railroad southeast of Summerville also showed a right-lateral offset of 4.5 ± 0.3 m (14.76 ± 0.98 ft) on the track.
The Old White Meeting House near Summerville, Dorchester County, South Carolina was reduced to ruins.
Major damage occurred as far away as Tybee Island, Georgia, which is more than 60 miles away.
Structural damage was reported several hundred miles from Charleston, including in central Alabama, central Ohio, eastern Kentucky, southern Virginia and western West Virginia.

Additionally, the South Carolina Emergency Management Division (SCEMD) has been created to plan disaster mitigation as well as respond to current disasters in order to reduce property damage and save lives.
Local photographer George LaGrange Cook took a series of photographs of the city after the quake, publishing them as Cook's Earthquake Views of Charleston and Vicinity.
A collection of his work is held by the Gibbes Museum of Art in the city.
The quake was even felt in cities as far as Boston and Chicago, where plaster fell from ceilings in upper floors of some buildings.
The most prominent damage was done to buildings constructed out of brick, amounting to 81% of building damage.
The damage was assessed to be between $5 million and $6 million.

1893 Brisbane flood
The 1893 Brisbane flood, occasionally called the Great Flood of 1893 or the Black February flood, occurred in 1893 in Brisbane, Queensland, Australia.
The Brisbane River burst its banks on three occasions in February 1893.
There was also a fourth flood later in the same year in June.
The second cyclone struck on 11 February 1893, causing relatively minor flooding compared to the first flood.
When the third cyclone came on 19 February 1893, it was almost as devastating as the first, and it left up to one third of Brisbane's residents homeless.
For the first flood, Crohamhurst recorded an all-time Australian record of 907 millimetres (35.7 in) of rain in a 24-hour period.
The water surge was recorded on the Port Office gauge (now the City gauge) as being 8.35 metres (27 feet, 5 inches) above the low tide level.
The February 1893 floods were the second and third highest water levels ever recorded at the City gauge, the highest being the January 1841 flood at 8.43 metres (27 feet, 8 inches).
The 1893 floods were preceded by two notable yet less severe floods in 1887 and 1890.
Samuel Griffith was the Premier of Queensland during the Black February period, although in March 1893 (shortly after the floods) he resigned in order to join the Supreme Court of Queensland.
In 1901 the Commonwealth of Australia was formed, at which time Queensland became a State.
The area was under the jurisdiction of several local governments (the present City of Brisbane being formed by their amalgamation in 1925).
John McMaster was Mayor of Brisbane Municipal Council, which contained the City Centre, and was the most important of the local government authorities.
The most flooded suburb of what was to become the City of Brisbane was Rocklea.
Both of the bridges that crossed the river, the Victoria Bridge and the Albert Bridge at Indooroopilly were destroyed.

The Victoria Bridge, which was an iron bridge with a turning span to allow traffic to go upriver, was partially destroyed on Monday 6 February 1893, when the northern half of the bridge was washed away.
A local businessman who would later become Premier, Robert Philp had a photo album (a very expensive item at the time) of the floods, which survives today.
The seven miners killed included Thomas Wright (Mine Manager) and George Wright who were both sons of the owner.
The other five miners were Andrew Smart, Patrick McQuade, John McQuade (son of Patrick), Charles Walker, and Mathew Cuthbertson.
Henry Plantagenet Somerset (1852–1936), was a landowner in the area where the Stanley River and the Upper Brisbane River meet.

Caboonbah meant "big rock" in the local indigenous language, and it was built 60 feet (18 metres) higher than the rock cliff (Weldon's Knob) which was the location of the previous highest flood mark, from the 1890 flood.
Somerset, realizing that people downriver where in great danger sent one of his workers, Henry (Harry) Winwood to Esk to send a telegraph to warn them.
The telegraph sent warned the Brisbane General Post Office that Brisbane, Ipswich, Goodna, Lowood and other areas were in danger.
The Brisbane General Post Office only posted the warning on a single noticeboard, and it went almost completely unheeded.
On 17 February, another cyclone crossed the Queensland coast near Bundaberg to drench the already saturated Brisbane River catchment.
Somerset observed that the Brisbane River was flooded in similar levels to the first flood of the Stanley River.
William (Billy) Mateer, of Eidsvold (Dalgangel Station) was Somerset's most talented horseman, and he was selected to undertake this dangerous mission.
Somerset and his men had to arrange for a dangerous crossing of the already flooded Brisbane River, with Mateer sent on with the only surviving horse (called Lunatic).
Mateer survived the hazardous journey to North Pine, and delivered Somerset's message, which was again sadly ignored.
Whilst the warnings went unheeded, as a result of these heroic efforts, Caboonbah Station was made an official flood warning station, with a telegraph line to Esk.
In modern times, Caboonbah Homestead was restored and used as a museum.

The site was first suggested for the location of a dam by Henry Somerset, after the 1893 floods, and he championed its construction when he was elected to parliament in 1904, where he served for 16 years as the Member for Stanley.
Construction of the dam was not started until 1933, and it was finally finished in 1953.
The site had been identified in 1933, by the Bureau of Industry.
The same day that the notice of Billy Mateer's death appeared in the newspaper, there was also a major announcement that the Queensland Government had approved the construction of Somerset Dam.
By 1959, it was believed that the Brisbane River system was regulated.
By the 1970s, the social memory of the 1893 floods had all but vanished.

During the American colonial period and after independence in 1946, barangays were called barrios and barangay leaders were called barrio lieutenants.
In 1991, the position took its present name and form with amendments to the Local Government Code.
Apart from performing many official government duties, they also execute minor judicial powers as part of the Barangay Justice System, such as settling disputes between neighbors.
